newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Gold - W. Australia miners hit by royalty.
newsitem.headline: Australia Gold - W. Australia miners hit by royalty.

text.p: For the first time, Australia's most prolific gold producing state, Western Australia, will see a gold royalty introduced.
The decision to apply the levy on the mining industry was confirmed in the state's 1997/98 (July-June) budget released earlier on Thursday, although the plan lacked details.
A royalty would bring Western Australia more in line with gold miners in other states, which have shouldered government levies for some time.

Queensland has a 2.75 percent gross royalty, while in New South Wales a smelter levy of four percent is equal to about a two percent gross royalty. The Northern Territory has an 18 percent net profit royalty.
old miners, led in part by Gwalia Consolidated Ltd managing director Peter Lalor, have vowed to fight the royalty on the grounds the industry can ill afford it.

Gold prices, at around A$443 an ounce, are hovering at their lowest level in years at a time when near-surface gold deposits are becoming exhausted forcing the miners to dig deeper, raising operating costs.
Lalor said one idea being discussed was to enable a royalty to kick in at a certain gold price and not before.
In whatever form, the royalty must still pass both upper and lower houses of the Western Australia state parliament.
"We are going to lobby against it," Lalor said.

"What the state government fails to realise is that in its attempt to raise more revenue, measures such as the introduction of a gold royalty will have a far more deleterious effect on the whole economy than the simple increase in revenue of A$70 million," Adrienne Wright, executive officer of the Association of Mining and Exploration Companies (Inc) (AMEC).

Wright said that estimates from a recent study funded by AMEC indicate that a royalty on a scale outlined in March by state premier Richard Court would cost gold miners over A$500 million in lost production and at least A$200 million in lost investments in the state.
Under a previously tabled royalty programme, the levy would start at 1.25 percent on January 1, 1998, rising to 2.5 percent by July 1999.
Court has said the levy is needed to offset shortfalls in Federal funding in the 1997/98 (July/June) fiscal year.
"A gold royalty is not the way to solve the state government's revenue problems," Wright said.

Western Australian gold miners have successfully fought off calls for a royalty for years, citing the jobs that accompany the ability to operate unhindered by the need to contribute directly to state coffers.
